public import Mathlib.Algebra.Polynomial.Degree.Defs
public import Mathlib.Algebra.Polynomial.Eval.Defs
public import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Defs

@[expose] public section

open Polynomial

/-!
This file introduces some common assumptions made on polynomials in certain conjectures.
Note that the terminology is non-standard.
-/

/--
**Bunyakovsky condition**
A condition on polynomials in the Schinzel and Bunyakovsky conjectures.
Holds for nonconstant irreducible polynomial with positive leading coefficient.
-/
def BunyakovskyCondition (f : ℤ[X]) : Prop :=
  1 ≤ f.degree ∧ Irreducible f ∧ 0 < f.leadingCoeff

/--
**Schinzel condition**
A condition on sets of polynomials in the Schinzel and Bunyakovsky conjectures.
Holds if for every prime $p$ there exists a natural $n$ such that for every polynomial $f$ in the set, $p$ does not divide $f(n)$.
-/
def SchinzelCondition (fs : Finset ℤ[X]) : Prop :=
  ∀ p : ℕ, p.Prime → ∃ n : ℕ, ∀ f ∈ fs, ¬(p : ℤ) ∣ f.eval (n : ℤ)

findings.description: Downstream use site in FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/BatemanHornConjecture.lean: BatemanHornConstant uses the default `∏'`, which is an unconditional product over arbitrary finite subsets of primes. The Bunyakovsky and Schinzel conditions do not guarantee this stronger convergence. For the admissible singleton {X² + 1}, the factors are 1 at p = 2 and 1 ∓ 1/(p−1) at odd primes according to p modulo 4. Consequently, the sum of their absolute deviations from 1 diverges. The ordered product nevertheless converges to a positive value C ≈ 1.37281, so an unconditional limit cannot exist. Mathlib therefore assigns this tprod its default value 1. The Lean BatemanHornConstant is then 1/2, whereas the source's degree-normalized constant is C/2 ≈ 0.68640. This changes the conjectured asymptotic. Neither definition in the reviewed library file needs changing.
findings.source_evidence: The cited Wikipedia article, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bateman%E2%80%93Horn_conjecture, defines the constant by the prime Euler product. Its referenced survey, Aletheia-Zomlefer–Fukshansky–Garcia, arXiv:1807.08899v4 (LaTeX read via https://arxiv.org/e-print/1807.08899), explicitly states in 'Convergence of the product': 'The product that defines the Bateman–Horn constant need not converge absolutely.' Its quadratic example gives the factors above and the coefficient 0.68640…. Mathlib/Topology/Algebra/InfiniteSum/Defs.lean defines default HasProd using all finite subsets and proves tprod_eq_one_of_not_multipliable.
findings.suggested_fix: In BatemanHornConstant, replace `∏' p : {p : ℕ // p.Prime}, ...` with `∏'[SummationFilter.conditional {p : ℕ // p.Prime}] p : {p : ℕ // p.Prime}, ...`, keeping the existing factors and degree prefactor. This ordered-product replacement elaborates in /workspace/review/bh_diagnostics.lean. An equivalent repair is a limit of products over primes below an increasing cutoff.

findings.description: In the same downstream file, the theorem's docstring says that `ω_p/p` is the number of residue classes where a polynomial vanishes. The number is ω_p, represented by OmegaP; ω_p/p is their proportion. The definition of OmegaP and the displayed Euler factor use the correct quantity.
findings.source_evidence: The 'Definition' section of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bateman%E2%80%93Horn_conjecture defines N(p) as the number of solutions modulo p, and uses N(p)/p in the Euler factor. The cited survey arXiv:1807.08899v4 makes the same distinction.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'Here ω_p/p is the number of residue classes' with 'Here ω_p is the number of residue classes' in the theorem docstring.

reformulations.difference: Uses a natural witness and simultaneous nondivisibility of individual evaluations, rather than saying that the product of the polynomials has no fixed divisor greater than 1 on the integers or positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Divisibility of an integer-polynomial evaluation modulo p depends only on its input modulo p. Every integer residue has a natural representative, and adding p gives a positive representative. Since p is prime, it divides a finite product exactly when it divides one factor. Finally, every integer greater than 1 has a prime divisor. These give the exact no-fixed-divisor characterization, including the empty-family case. The integer-witness, positive-witness, product, and fixed-divisor iff statements were proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Uses irreducibility in ℤ[X], and counts natural inputs with prime absolute values, whereas the cited formulation uses rational irreducibility and positive inputs with positive prime values.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: SchinzelCondition {f} implies f.IsPrimitive, so Gauss's lemma equates integer and rational irreducibility. Positive degree and positive leading coefficient imply eventual positivity of f(n). Thus input zero and negative prime values contribute only finitely many exceptions. The irreducibility and infinitude iff components were proved in extra.lean and sign.lean.

reformulations.difference: Counts natural inputs, including zero, at which all absolute values are prime instead of positive inputs at which all values are positive primes.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every polynomial has positive leading coefficient, hence is eventually positive. Finiteness of the family supplies a common bound. Outside the resulting finite initial interval, the two predicates coincide. The full infinitude iff for arbitrary finite families, including the empty family, was proved as infinite_family_prime_iff in sign.lean.

reformulations.difference: Adds BunyakovskyCondition to the degree-one assumption, apparently imposing irreducibility beyond the source's positive-slope and local-admissibility assumptions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Local admissibility forces every polynomial to be primitive. A primitive degree-one integer polynomial is irreducible by Gauss's lemma and irreducibility of degree-one polynomials over ℚ. Thus the added irreducibility and degree lower bound are redundant; only positive leading coefficient remains. The exact hypotheses iff was proved as dickson_hypotheses_iff in extra.lean. The absolute-prime counting convention is also covered by sign.lean.

reformulations.difference: The unannotated input in the globally quantified hypothesis hs is inferred to be ℤ, and primality is tested on absolute values. This looks weaker than the usual positive-input, positive-prime formulation of H, but the global hypotheses are equivalent.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For an admissible family f_i, let D be the sum of degrees, let B be the product of primes at most 2D, and choose A ≥ 0 by CRT with every f_i(A) nonzero modulo those primes. Apply the integer/absolute-value hypothesis to both f_i(A+BX) and (−1)^(deg f_i) f_i(A−BX). This enlarged family is admissible: small primes are handled by A, while for p > 2D the union of roots has size at most 2D < p and B is invertible modulo p. Affine substitution preserves rational irreducibility, and admissibility ensures primitivity, giving the required integer irreducibility. Each successful integer t yields prime absolute values of the original family at A+B|t|. This map has finite fibers, so infinitely many natural arguments result; eventual positivity gives positive primes. The converse follows from the injection ℕ → ℤ. The empty family is trivial. This argument is detailed in review_notes.md, but was not formalized in Lean.

reformulations.difference: Separately from the incorrect constant reported above, replaces the source's logarithmic integral by x/(log x)^k and includes zero and absolute prime values in its counting function.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For fixed k, the integral from 2 to x of 1/(log t)^k is asymptotic to x/(log x)^k. Under the polynomial hypotheses, the counting conventions differ by only finitely many inputs. Since the intended constant is positive and x/(log x)^k tends to infinity, neither change alters the intended asymptotic.
